title: Pharmacy
goal: Describe your sore throat to the pharmacist and understand how to use what they give you.
twist: The pharmacist asks follow-up questions before recommending anything.
safety: This is a language task only. The product (Harbour Honey & Lemon lozenges) and its instructions are fictional and constructed for teaching. It is not medical advice. For a real health problem, ask a pharmacist or doctor.
note: Fictional dialogue constructed for teaching purposes.

start.speaker: Narrator
start.line: Language practice only, not medical advice. In this story you have had a sore throat since yesterday. You go to the pharmacy counter.

greet.speaker: Mr Okafor
greet.line: Good morning. How can I help?

options.text: Hi. I've got a sore throat. Can you recommend something for it?
options.feedback: Clear and polite. You named the problem and asked for a recommendation.

options.text: Give me the strongest medicine you have.
options.feedback: Grammatical, but it sounds demanding, and the pharmacist needs to know the problem first.
options.recast: I've got a sore throat. What do you recommend?

options.text: My throat is sick.
options.feedback: Mr Okafor understands. In English a throat isn't 'sick' — the usual phrase is 'I've got a sore throat'.

whatproblem.speaker: Mr Okafor
whatproblem.line: I can't give you anything without knowing what it's for. What's the problem?
whatproblem.slower: First, tell me the problem, please.

options.text: Sorry. I've got a sore throat.
options.feedback: Good recovery. A short apology and a clear description.

options.text: Does it matter? I'm just ill.
options.feedback: This sounds impatient. The pharmacist asks so they can give you the right thing.
options.recast: It's my throat. It's very sore.

options.text: My throat is hurting me since yesterday.
options.feedback: Understood. With 'since', English uses the present perfect: 'My throat has been hurting since yesterday', or simply 'I've had a sore throat since yesterday'.
options.recast: I've had a sore throat since yesterday.

whyask.speaker: Mr Okafor
whyask.line: It does matter. Different problems need different things. Is it your throat, your head, your stomach?

howlong.speaker: Mr Okafor
howlong.line: I see. How long have you had it?

build.prompt: Say that you have had it since yesterday.

nearMisses.feedback: Use 'since' with a starting point (yesterday, Monday). Use 'for' with a length of time (two days).
With 'since', use the present perfect: 'I've had it'.
Use 'I've had it since yesterday': present perfect + since + a starting point.

build.hint: How long? Start with 'I've had it'. Then since + a starting point.

options.text: I've had it since yesterday.
options.feedback: Correct and clear: present perfect + since + a starting point.

options.text: A while. Not sure. Maybe a long time, maybe not.
options.feedback: It is very vague, so the pharmacist can't use the answer.
options.recast: About a day. It started yesterday.

options.text: I have it since yesterday.
options.feedback: A very common error. With 'since', use the present perfect: 'I've had it since yesterday.'

vague.speaker: Mr Okafor
vague.line: Roughly, then. Did it start today, yesterday, or last week?

symptoms.speaker: Mr Okafor
symptoms.line: Do you have a temperature, or any trouble swallowing?
symptoms.slower: Are you hot? Is it hard to eat and drink?
symptoms.spell: Swallowing: S, W, A, L, L, O, W, I, N, G. It means food or drink going down your throat.

options.text: No temperature. It hurts a bit when I swallow, but I can eat and drink.
options.feedback: Very useful answer. You answered both questions with clear detail.

options.text: Sorry, what does 'swallowing' mean?
options.feedback: Good repair strategy. It's fine to ask about one word.

options.text: Why are you asking so many questions?
options.feedback: This sounds rude. Pharmacists ask follow-up questions to keep you safe.
options.recast: Sorry, why do you need to know?

options.text: I don't have temperature, only hurt when I swallowing.
options.feedback: Understood. Say 'a temperature', and 'it hurts when I swallow'.
options.recast: I don't have a temperature. It only hurts when I swallow.

swallow.speaker: Mr Okafor
swallow.line: Swallowing is when food or drink goes down your throat, like this. Is that painful?

whyquestions.speaker: Mr Okafor
whyquestions.line: I need to check it isn't something more serious. It only takes a minute.

medicine.speaker: Mr Okafor
medicine.line: And are you taking any other medicine at the moment?
medicine.slower: Do you take other medicine now?

options.text: No, I'm not taking any other medicine.
options.feedback: Clear answer to an important safety question.

options.text: That's private.
options.feedback: Grammatical, but this is a normal and important question at a pharmacy. Answering helps them keep you safe.
options.recast: No, I'm not taking anything else.

options.text: No, I not take other medicines.
options.feedback: Use 'I'm not taking' (or 'I don't take') for now.
options.recast: No, I'm not taking any other medicine.

private.speaker: Mr Okafor
private.line: I understand. I only ask because some medicines don't mix well. You can just say yes or no.

recommend.speaker: Mr Okafor
recommend.line: OK. These honey and lemon lozenges might help. You suck them slowly. You can have one every three hours, but no more than six in a day. It's all on the box.
recommend.slower: Take one sweet every three hours. Not more than six in one day. Read the box.
recommend.spell: Lozenges: L, O, Z, E, N, G, E, S. Small sweets for your throat.

options.text: So one every three hours, and no more than six a day. Is that right?
options.feedback: Excellent. You checked the instructions by repeating the numbers.

options.text: Sorry, how often should I take them?
options.feedback: Good repair. Numbers in instructions are easy to miss.

options.text: Fine. I'll take lots so it goes away faster.
options.feedback: This is a safety problem. Always follow the instructions on the box, and ask the pharmacist if you are unsure.
options.recast: OK. How many can I have in a day?

options.text: One for three hours?
options.feedback: Use 'every': 'one every three hours'. 'For three hours' means a length of time.

repeatdose.speaker: Mr Okafor
repeatdose.line: One lozenge every three hours. Not more than six in a day.

nomore.speaker: Mr Okafor
nomore.line: Please don't. No more than six in a day. More won't help it go faster.

doctor.speaker: Mr Okafor
doctor.line: Drink plenty of water, too. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
doctor.slower: Drink lots of water. Any more questions?

options.text: What if it doesn't get better? Should I see a doctor?
options.feedback: A very good question to ask. Knowing when to see a doctor is important.

options.text: No, that's all. Thanks very much.
options.feedback: Polite and natural. It is also a good idea to ask when to see a doctor.

options.text: Are you sure you know what you're doing?
options.feedback: This questions the pharmacist's skill and sounds insulting. If you are worried, ask when to see a doctor.
options.recast: Should I see a doctor if it doesn't get better?

options.text: When I must go to doctor?
options.feedback: Question word order: 'When should I see a doctor?' And use 'a' before 'doctor'.
options.recast: When should I see a doctor?

advice.speaker: Mr Okafor
advice.line: If it isn't better in a few days, or you feel worse, see a doctor. And you can always come back and ask me.

end.speaker: Narrator
end.line: You explained your problem, answered the pharmacist's questions and checked the instructions. Remember: this was a language task. For real health problems, ask a pharmacist or doctor.
end.summary: Task complete: problem described, follow-up questions answered, instructions checked. One sound to watch: the 'th' of 'throat' is the /θ/ sound — tongue lightly between the teeth, no 't'.
